c.tagline: A British Rock at the gates of the Mediterranean, ruled by wild monkeys.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps (Uber/Bolt) operate in Gibraltar; use the licensed white taxis at ranks, hotels and the border, or take the Rock Tour taxis. Pounds and euros are both usually accepted, though pounds give a better rate.

emergency.note: 999 and 112 both reach the emergency services (police, ambulance and fire).

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The Upper Rock macaques snatch food and bags — don't feed or touch them; otherwise only usual awareness in crowded Main Street on cruise-ship days.

hood_desc: Gibraltar's walkable historic core: pedestrianised Main Street's duty-free shops, Casemates Square, the cathedral and the Cable Car base station up the Rock. Best for first-timers who want everything on foot.

A modern waterfront marina lined with restaurants, bars, a casino and the floating five-star Sunborn yacht hotel; the territory's liveliest dining-and-nightlife scene, good for a social or romantic stay.
The flat eastern corridor by the airport and the Spanish border at La Línea, near Eastern Beach; a practical, well-connected base for airport access and longer or business stays.
lodging: Jasmine Coral Jay Boutique Boatel Ocean Village

water.note: The separate potable (desalinated) tap supply is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 7am to 9pm; the Cable Car operates about 9:30am-7:15pm (shorter hours in winter). There is no rail or metro.
transit.pay: Bus single fares are about £1.10 (a day pass is around £2.50), paid in cash to the driver in pounds; euros are usually accepted at a slightly worse rate. The Cable Car up the Rock is a separate ticket (about £19 return, or £38 including the Nature Reserve).

bus: Cross-border local buses from La Línea (Spain)

transit.m: Walk across the runway into town (~15-20 min on foot)
Bus route 5 to the town centre (~10 min)

tip.r: A service charge is often already included; otherwise rounding up or leaving ~10% for good service is appreciated.

landmarks: The Rock of Gibraltar (Upper Rock Nature Reserve)
The legendary limestone Pillar of Hercules soars 426 metres from the sea, honeycombed with caves and tunnels and patrolled by wild macaques.
Barbary Macaques at Apes' Den
Europe's only wild monkeys clamber over railings and rooftops at the cable-car middle station; legend says British Gibraltar endures while they remain.
St Michael's Cave
A cathedral-sized grotto of floodlit stalactites deep inside the Rock, spectacularly transformed by an immersive light show and used as a concert auditorium.
Great Siege Tunnels
Hand-hewn by British soldiers during the 1779-83 siege, these galleries carved through solid rock bristle with cannon embrasures overlooking the isthmus.
Europa Point and Trinity Lighthouse
Gibraltar's southernmost tip stares across the Strait to Morocco's Rif mountains, beside a red-and-white lighthouse and the striking Ibrahim-al-Ibrahim Mosque.
Skywalk and Windsor Suspension Bridge
A glass platform perched 340 metres above the sea and a 71-metre bridge slung across a gorge deliver Gibraltar's most knee-trembling viewpoints.
Moorish Castle
The crenellated Tower of Homage, rebuilt in 1333, has flown flags of Moors, Spain and Britain and still dominates the northern approach to town.
Gibraltar Cable Car
Six minutes of soaring ascent from Grand Parade to the Rock's summit terraces, where views sweep from Africa to the Costa del Sol.
Main Street and Grand Casemates Square
A quirky British-Mediterranean high street of pubs, duty-free shops and bobbies runs from the lively former barracks square through the old town.
O'Hara's Battery
At the Rock's highest point, this preserved 9.2-inch gun emplacement commands a staggering 360-degree panorama over two continents and two seas.

train.note: Gibraltar has no railway. The nearest station is San Roque-La Línea in Spain, a few kilometres north, on the Renfe network (https://www.renfe.com/es/en) with connections at Algeciras and Bobadilla toward Málaga, Madrid and Seville - services are sparse, so most people use the bus.

intl.to: La Línea de la Concepción & Algeciras (Spain) - across the land frontier
intl.op: Spanish regional bus operators — tickets at the La Línea terminal

bus.note: You walk across the frontier - and across the airport runway - to La Línea, where the Spanish bus station has frequent services to Algeciras, Málaga, Seville and Tarifa for the Morocco ferries. Queues at the border can be long, particularly at shift-change times. Gibraltar's own buses cover the Rock itself. Carry your passport.

intl.to: Tanger Med (Morocco) - ~1h30, sailings limited and irregular

intl.op: Gibraltar-Algeciras ferry operators — tickets at the terminal

ferry.note: Gibraltar's own ferry links have been thin for years - the Tangier service has run intermittently, so verify it before planning around it. The reliable Morocco crossings leave from Tarifa (35 minutes to Tangier Ville) and Algeciras (to Tanger Med), both an hour or less away by bus from La Línea. Bring your passport for any of these.
